final_proof:
Let \(s[P]=\{s(x):x\in P\}\). By the axioms of a Peano structure, \(0\in P\), the map \(s\) maps \(P\) into \(P\), \(0\notin s[P]\), and the induction axiom holds: if \(A\subseteq P\) contains \(0\) and satisfies \(s(a)\in A\) for every \(a\in A\), then \(A=P\). (The injectivity axiom for \(s\) is not needed here.)

Define
\[
A=\{0\}\cup s[P].
\]
Because \(0\in P\) and \(s[P]\subseteq P\), we have \(A\subseteq P\); moreover, \(0\in A\). If \(a\in A\), then in particular \(a\in P\). Consequently \(s(a)\in s[P]\subseteq A\). Thus \(A\) is closed under \(s\). The induction axiom therefore gives
\[
P=A=\{0\}\cup s[P].
\]
It follows that every element of \(P\) which is not in \(s[P]\) must equal \(0\). Conversely, the Peano axiom \(0\notin s[P]\), together with \(0\in P\), shows that \(0\in P\setminus s[P]\). Hence
\[
P\setminus s[P]=\{0\}.
\]
Therefore \(P\setminus s[P]\) is a singleton, and \(0\) is the unique non-successor element of \(P\).
